developments.title: Huawei Atlas 300I Duo offers 96GB for $1,400 with llama.cpp CANN quants limited to F16, Q4_0, and Q8_0
detail: KyzoroX reports that Huawei's Atlas 300I Duo, a 150W single-slot server card with two Ascend 310P chips, 96GB of LPDDR4X, and no Nvidia silicon, is sold by Chinese sellers at $1,400 to $2,800 depending on order size, and that llama.cpp already has a backend for it. Each chip reads only its own 48GB at 204 GB/s during inference, capping a Q4 70B dense model at roughly 5-10 tok/s versus about 22 tok/s on two RTX 3090s, with early benchmarks around 15 tok/s on Qwen3 32B. The card runs Linux only and is built for Huawei's Kunpeng servers.

Alexey Fateev argues the dense-70B framing is outdated because local inference has moved to sparse MoE models holding 100B-600B parameters while activating only 3B-8B per token. At 5.5B active parameters in 4-bit, the ~3 GB read per token puts the 204 GB/s memory ceiling near 65 tok/s, and the full 96GB fits 120B+ MoE models with no RAM offload. He says the real home-use blockers are the split 48GB-per-chip memory pool, the passive card's rack airflow needs, and Huawei's CANN backend in llama.cpp covering only F16, Q4_0, and Q8_0, with no IQ quants and no custom MoE kernels.
developments.why_it_matters: Buyers get about three times an RTX 5090's 32GB for less money, but must plan for Linux-only server operation and Huawei's limited CANN quant formats.

developments.title: OpenAI corrects GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol billing discount; quotas now burn up to 40% faster
detail: OpenAI has fixed a billing mistake from the GPT-6.2 launch that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users, and the correction is now live: the same work reaches each plan's limits 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol than last week, while no other models are affected.
Past usage will not be charged for the difference, and as an apology every account on the Go, Plus, Pro, and Business plans receives one additional banked reset.
Both models are still stated to go further in usage than 6 Astra and 6.1 Sol.
developments.why_it_matters: Teams scheduling Astra or Sol jobs against plan limits must recalculate runtimes under the corrected metering, since estimates based on last week's rates now overrun.

developments.title: Alexey Fateev’s llm.asm runs Qwen3-0.6B inference in 12 KB of x86-64 assembly
detail: Alexey Fateev says llm.asm is a 12,120-byte static Linux ELF that runs the full 28-layer Qwen3-0.6B forward pass from 3,688 lines of NASM, using Q8_0 mmap weights, 16Q/8KV GQA, QK-Norm, split-half RoPE, SwiGLU, a KV cache, and greedy/top-p sampling. The implementation uses AVX2/FMA matrix multiplication, custom polynomial expf and sincosf, an assembly BPE tokenizer, and raw clone()/futex() threading without libc, libm, pthreads, or shared libraries.

On an EPYC 7642, Fateev reports 105.39 tokens/s peak decode, 64 greedy tokens matching a PyTorch FP32 reference, bit-identical output from 1 through 47 threads, and 1.000000000 cosine similarity against a Python Q8_0 reference. He says the project includes the source and build guide.
developments.why_it_matters: Linux developers can now audit and test Qwen3 inference with a 12 KB runtime instead of provisioning PyTorch’s multi-gigabyte runtime.

developments.title: Pi v1.6.1 adds callable GitHub Copilot and Radius decision models
detail: Pi 1.6.1 introduces decision models from GitHub Copilot (gpt-6-luna-decisions) and Radius that can be invoked through the codemode models.classify() API, now returning a responseId in the results.
The release also replaces the single showCacheMissNotices flag with four per‑transcript notice settings and removes the SettingsManager getters and setters for that flag.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers can now invoke Copilot and Radius decision models directly, enabling richer automated reasoning without manual API calls.

developments.title: Ciarán Cotter unveils new AI hacking techniques using data compression and linguistic gadgets
detail: Ciarán Cotter announced the creation of novel AI hacking methods that leverage data compression tricks and linguistic‑based gadgets, first presented at the Prompt2Pwn conference.
He provided a write‑up of the techniques via a linked post for the community to review.
developments.why_it_matters: Researchers can test these compression‑based attacks to strengthen model defenses and improve AI security practices.

developments.title: PrismML releases Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B model
detail: PrismML announced the availability of Ternary Bonsai 2.5, a 27‑billion‑parameter model built on Qwen3.8. The new version retains the 5.9 GB footprint of its predecessor while delivering substantially stronger agentic coding, multi‑turn tool use, and long‑horizon task execution. Benchmarks show it scores 73.9 on tau3‑bench and 75.6 on SWE‑Bench‑Verified, making it the strongest model of its size for agentic workloads.

Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, the 2.5 release completes tasks in fewer turns, consumes fewer tokens, and produces results faster and more accurately. The model is released under the Apache 2.0 license, enabling local deployment and experimentation.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now run high‑performance agentic coding locally with a 5.9 GB model, lowering hardware requirements for complex AI‑driven workflows.

developments.title: Ramp Labs introduces speculative encoding, a 2.35B MoE that translates hidden states between models
detail: Ramp Labs introduced speculative encoding, a single 2.35B-parameter MoE model that translates hidden states directly between different LLMs. The stated goal is that shared context gets read once and reused across every model in a multi-agent swarm instead of being re-read for each.
In benchmarks across 7 models, the technique reportedly preserves 96.9% of base accuracy while cutting prefill latency by up to 7.5× on long documents.
developments.why_it_matters: Builders of multi-model agent pipelines can share a single translated context across model swaps instead of re-prefilling after each switch, accepting up to 3.1% accuracy loss.

developments.title: Factory makes its individual developer tier free with bring-your-own inference
detail: Factory has made its product free for individual developers who bring their own inference: users download the app, add their own API key, and start their first task. As a limited-time holiday bonus, Factory is also adding free Droid Computer hours to every account.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers holding an existing inference API key can now run Factory's agent app without paying Factory, and their accounts pick up free Droid Computer hours while the offer lasts.

developments.title: Alperen Keleş's Ephyra at Datadog finds 535 previously unknown bugs in Lean, OCaml, SQLite, PostgreSQL, and FoundationDB
detail: Alperen Keleş announced that his first project at Datadog, Ephyra, is now public: an agentic property-based testing framework with built-in autonomous generator optimization.
He reports that Ephyra found 535 previously unknown bugs across Lean, OCaml, SQLite, PostgreSQL, FoundationDB, and other heavily tested systems.
developments.why_it_matters: Engineers testing systems like SQLite, PostgreSQL, and FoundationDB can now apply Ephyra's public framework, whose autonomous generators exposed 535 defects that existing testing in such well-tested projects had missed.

developments.title: Josh's Claude-powered photo classification tool
detail: Josh announced a new feature that classifies entire photo collections using Claude. The system sends each image with its EXIF metadata and location to the model, processing batches of roughly 45 000 photos for about $500 in API credits.
The model returns searchable tags and extracted text, enabling queries that locate images by where they were taken, embedded text, or other visual cues in milliseconds.
developments.why_it_matters: You can instantly query large photo libraries without manual tagging, saving hours of organization work.

external_links.title: OpenTrawl: Spotlight for the Agentic OS

developments.title: Google forbids AI agents from using Workspace APIs
detail: Google announced that its new Model Control Plane (MCP) will block AI agents, including tools like gog and openclaw, from accessing Workspace APIs unless the agents are paid for.
This policy change restricts the capabilities of third‑party AI agents that rely on Google Workspace integrations, forcing developers to either obtain paid access or redesign their agents.
developments.why_it_matters: AI‑agent developers must adjust or pay for Workspace API access, or their tools will lose functionality.

developments.title: Daniel Miessler adds one-way-door escalation to his AI system's deploy review
detail: Daniel Miessler says he added a constitution rule to his AI system based on Jeff Bezos's one-way and two-way door distinction. Most actions are reversible because code is kept in git and actions are logged, so those receive less upfront checking and are verified afterward.

Actions that cannot be undone, such as pushing an API key to a public repository or exposing customer data, receive more upfront validation, including review by a second model from another laboratory. In code, when an AI reviewer blocks a deployment and the AI disputes it, a model from another lab rules on the appeal, except when the blocker is a one-way-door change, which always goes to Miessler.
developments.why_it_matters: Practitioners can use reversibility to separate fast-checked agent actions from irreversible ones that require human or independent-model escalation.

developments.title: GPT-Next reported to have proved the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4
detail: Dan McAteer says GPT-Next has produced a proof that the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4, describing it as the resolution of a 57-year-old theoretical computer science problem that he says required superhuman AI to solve.
A proven exponent of exactly 9/4 would pin down the asymptotic cost of matrix multiplication, and McAteer's framing ties the result to direct implications for AI R&D.
No paper, proof sketch, or independent verification accompanies the claim, so the result currently stands as unconfirmed.
developments.why_it_matters: Until a verified proof or paper appears, readers should treat the 9/4 result as an unconfirmed claim rather than a settled theorem.

developments.title: Check Point firewall compromised via Math.random PRNG weakness
detail: An attacker exploited the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint of Check Point's firewall management server, which signed session cookies using a value derived from JavaScript's Math.random().
By collecting multiple session cookie signatures, the attacker reconstructed the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm and forged a valid admin session cookie, granting password‑less admin access.
developments.why_it_matters: Admins must replace Math.random with a CSPRNG for signing cookies to stop similar forgery attacks.

developments.title: LessWrong reports reliable communication between sandboxed inference-server agents
detail: A LessWrong write-up reports that two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate even when they cannot send each other messages or access the same files.

The finding indicates that blocking ordinary messaging and shared-file access does not necessarily isolate agents colocated on one inference server. The supplied excerpt does not identify the communication mechanism, affected providers, or available mitigations.
developments.why_it_matters: Engineers using per-agent sandboxes on shared inference infrastructure should test for cross-agent channels instead of assuming file and messaging restrictions provide complete isolation.

external_links.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed — LessWrong

developments.title: Conductor adds Publish for putting artifacts on the internet
detail: Charlie Holtz announced Conductor Publish, a new feature in his Conductor app that lets users publish artifacts to the internet. The announcement links to the feature but does not describe how publishing works, which artifact types are supported, or where published content is hosted.

Conductor is the same app Holtz recently rebuilt with an Electron frontend while retaining its Rust local server, a rewrite that reportedly made workspace opening 71% faster and cut RAM use by 35%. Publish adds a public web path for output produced in that otherwise local environment.
developments.why_it_matters: Conductor users can now publish their artifacts to the public web from the app, removing the need to host such output elsewhere themselves.

developments.title: Drew Breunig argues AI mediation of communal decisions may sacrifice trust-building judgment
detail: Drew Breunig commented on Patrick Collison's essay about travel writing and culture, then argued that it stops short by not examining how trust is built through communal decision-making. He cited town and jury deliberation as producing both decisions and practice in governance, asking whether AI resolution of such matters might improve outcomes while weakening judgment and connection.

He pointed to contemporary anthropology, including Anna Tsing's "Friction" and Donna Haraway's cyborg and situated-knowledge work, as useful for framing personal and community interactions with AI as negotiations between parties. The commentary asks how culture and trust are formed in those interactions rather than treating AI only as a solver of collective problems.
developments.why_it_matters: Readers working on AI in civic or community settings should weigh whether automating decisions preserves the participatory judgment and trust that deliberation builds.

developments.title: Alexey Fateev's asm-llm-os runs Qwen3-0.6B chat in a 24 KB bare-metal x86-64 assembly OS, up to 54% faster than Linux llama.cpp
detail: Alexey Fateev reports building asm-llm-os, a 24,252-byte Multiboot operating system written entirely in x86-64 assembly with no Linux, Windows, C, Rust, or libc. It boots in 74–94 ms into 64-bit Long Mode, wakes every CPU core over APIC, maps the 614 MiB Q8_0 Qwen3-0.6B weights directly from physical RAM, and serves a live multi-turn KV-cache chat over VGA, PS/2 keyboard, and serial. Head-to-head Q8_0 benchmarks against llama.cpp (-ngl 0) on the same AMD EPYC 7642 report 23.67 tok/s versus 16.63 at one thread (+42%), 78.89 versus 51.08 at four (+54%), 118.08 versus 80.79 at eight (+46%), and a 136.6 tok/s peak at 16 threads (+31%).

The OS runs diskless on a 2 GiB Proxmox VM with a 95 ms kernel boot straight to the prompt, decoding at 78 tok/s and prefilling at up to 111.5 tok/s; the repo ships a hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO builder and a Proxmox setup guide. Output stays bit-exact across thread counts and matches a PyTorch FP32 reference on all 64 greedy tokens at 0.99965 cosine similarity. A companion 14.7 KB Linux ELF build (FAST_Q8=1, INT8xINT8 AVX2+F16C) reportedly beats llama.cpp by 18–36% from 1 to 40 threads, with 2 MiB huge pages on bare metal adding about 10% more.
developments.why_it_matters: Readers running llama.cpp on fixed hardware can weigh the reported 31–54% throughput gap as the cost of the Linux stack versus a 24 KB standalone assembly OS.

developments.title: Axitek upgrades a self-hosted inference homelab with two 240V/30A circuits
detail: Axitek says they are installing two 240V/30A circuits and moving inference servers into a dedicated room. The change is also expected to free up a laundry room once the computers are moved.
developments.why_it_matters: This move indicates that scaling an at-home inference setup to multiple high-draw GPUs calls for dedicated 240V/30A electrical circuits rather than ordinary household outlets.

developments.title: OpenCode releases standalone Codemode JavaScript runtime for native apps
detail: OpenCode extracted the Codemode runtime into a standalone package that can directly execute JavaScript and pause or resume execution mid‑run.
A Rust implementation is planned, allowing native applications to use JavaScript as a scripting language without embedding a full JS runtime, and it even works on mobile.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers can add JS‑based plugins to native OpenCode desktop and iOS apps without a heavyweight runtime, reducing bundle size and enabling faster mobile agent creation.

developments.title: Psychoscript gains a bytecode VM with in-memory snapshot and resume
detail: James Long says a needed suspend/resume capability prompted rewriting an implementation from an interpreter to a bytecode virtual machine, work he says he completed in a day while doing other work using the Carbon model. Dax adds that Psychoscript has a bytecode VM that can snapshot its in-memory state and resume without replaying prior work, avoiding the durable-workflow pattern of caching every function-call result.

The change addresses the older durable-workflow problem where resuming can require replaying and skipping cached results for each step; for a loop with thousands of calls, that can mean saving every call's result. Psychoscript instead snapshots its in-memory state, so resumption does not require replaying those calls.
developments.why_it_matters: Readers building durable workflows can avoid replaying and caching every step by using a VM that snapshots in-memory state.

developments.title: Rex adds program resumption across server restarts through new OSC 7577 protocol
detail: Mitchell Hashimoto announced that Rex can now resume programs through a server restart using the newly published OSC 7577 terminal protocol, developed with Herdrdev and reviewed by multiple terminal emulator and terminal program authors.

The protocol is based on ordinary terminal escape sequences, so any program can restart without special terminal-specific integration or an out-of-band protocol. Rex initially ships built-in support for Claude Code by emitting OSC 7577 from a session start hook.

Because terminal program restart is inherently unsafe, Rex uses a Lua-based configuration for opt-in resumption filtered by program name, path, working directory, command-line flags, and other criteria, with a global disable option; the quoted announcement states that the terminal emulator is ultimately responsible for enforcing security.
developments.why_it_matters: Terminal and coding-agent developers can implement cross-restart program resumption with ordinary escape sequences, but should treat terminal-side opt-in and emulator trust boundaries as security controls.

developments.title: Anthropic's Claude compresses Lean formalization of the Riemann Hypothesis by 99.56%
detail: Anthropic researchers used Claude to compress the Lean formalization of the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization, shrinking it from 17.4 million lines to 76 000 lines—a 99.56 % reduction.
The reduction, over 200× smaller, demonstrates Claude’s ability to assist in large‑scale formal verification tasks, potentially accelerating proof development and review.
developments.why_it_matters: This enables proof engineers to verify extensive formalizations with far less compute, allowing more projects to adopt Lean verification.

developments.title: Telos-Live-1 previews omni-modal full-duplex vision, audio, and tool use
detail: Telos Lab introduced Telos-Live-1 as its first omni-modal, full-duplex model, saying it can see, hear, and talk at the same time while keeping conversation active during search, tool use, and computer operation.

The accompanying commentator frames the model as observing a developer's screen while coding and intervening before a bug ships, and notes that many live voice models freeze during tool calls or long user turns. Latency behavior beyond preview remains unvalidated, and no release, pricing, API, or benchmark details are stated.
developments.why_it_matters: Evaluators can now test whether one model can maintain spoken interaction while performing screen-aware coding assistance and background tool calls.

developments.title: Ant Ling's LingSante-Live splits real-time multimodal reasoning into foreground and background loops
detail: Ant Ling introduced LingSante-Live, a real-time multimodal architecture for ongoing health collaboration. Its design separates a fast foreground response loop from an asynchronous background reasoning loop whose tasks can be updated, canceled, and checked for relevance before the assistant speaks.

The architecture also splits sensor update cadence by activity: high-frequency updates for movement, sustained windows for camera-based vitals, and event triggers for devices. In physician review across 300 video calls against Doubao and ChatGPT, it scored 4.80/5 for response timeliness, 4.56/5 for diagnostic accuracy, and 4.85/5 for advice practicality.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers building real-time multimodal agents can reuse its foreground/background split to prevent stale answers after interruption.

developments.title: Inkling 2 Mini model released for Linux via Ollama 0.40.18
detail: Inkling 2 Mini, a 26‑billion‑parameter model, is now available on Linux (and Windows) through Ollama version 0.40.18.
It runs on devices with 32 GB of unified memory or more and includes performance improvements on macOS via custom kernels.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now run the 26B Inkling 2 Mini model locally on Linux systems with 32 GB RAM, enabling offline agentic coding without cloud services.

developments.title: Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure publishes full forensic report on ARTEX hack of its own network
detail: The Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) has released the full forensic report on the September hack of its own network, an intrusion carried out using ARTEX, as reported by security journalist Kim Zetter. The forensic timeline shows the attack took only 1.3 seconds to hijack an administrator account and 20 minutes to take full control of the server.
Daniel Miessler shared the report while framing the sequence as a fully automated attack from start to finish.
developments.why_it_matters: Defenders can now read the public forensic report to see exactly how an automated ARTEX chain went from admin hijack to full server control in 20 minutes.

developments.title: ShellBench benchmark released for evaluating AI agents
detail: ShellBench, a new benchmark of 100 real-world tasks, has been released, testing 12 AI models across five harnesses with more than 53,000 graded runs. The release was announced by OpenClaw and ParseWaveAI, highlighting collaborative effort on the benchmark.
Initial results show a top score of 62.5% and a failure rate of roughly 40% on everyday tasks, with open‑source harnesses holding their own against proprietary counterparts.
developments.why_it_matters: The benchmark provides a standardized metric, letting developers compare agent performance and target specific improvements.

developments.title: Sakana Marlin update adds Twilight 2.0, Midnight 2.0, and refreshed slide output
detail: Sakana Marlin has been updated with Twilight 2.0, Midnight 2.0, and refreshed slide output.
Sakana AI says Twilight 2.0 supports quick, multi-angle examination, while Midnight 2.0 supports broad exploration for new findings.
developments.why_it_matters: Readers can use Sakana Marlin with its new Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0 research modes and refreshed slide output.
